answer:
The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of the liquid becomes **equal to the pressure applied on its surface**.

At that temperature the vapour can push back the applied pressure, so bubbles of vapour form throughout the bulk of the liquid and rise to the surface, and the liquid boils.

Because the boiling point is fixed by the applied pressure, its value changes when that pressure changes. The **normal boiling point** is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of the liquid equals \(1\ \mathrm{atm} = 760\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\); for water it is \(373.15\ \mathrm{K}\), that is \(100\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\).

Dissolving a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the solvent at every temperature, so the solution has to be heated above \(T_b^0\) before its vapour pressure reaches the applied pressure. That rise is the elevation of boiling point,

\(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^0\)

answer:
**(A)** Vapour pressure

A colligative property is a property of a solution that depends only on the **number** of solute particles dissolved and not on their nature. There are exactly four of them: **lowering of vapour pressure**, **elevation of boiling point**, **depression of freezing point** and **osmotic pressure**.

Vapour pressure by itself is not one of these. The vapour pressure of a liquid is decided by the nature of the liquid and by the temperature - water and benzene have quite different vapour pressures at the same temperature - so it cannot depend on the number of particles alone. What is colligative is the **lowering** of vapour pressure produced by the solute,

\(\Delta P = P_1^0 - P_1 = P_1^0x_2\)

which contains only \(x_2\), the mole fraction of the solute.

The other three named quantities are colligative, and each is written in terms of the amount of solute alone:

\(\Delta T_f = K_fm\), \(\Delta T_b = K_bm\), \(\pi = MRT\)

answer:
**(A)** number of solute particles

A colligative property depends only on the number of solute particles present in a given amount of solvent, and not at all on what those particles are. One mole of urea and one mole of glucose dissolved in the same mass of water depress the freezing point by exactly the same amount, because each supplies the same number of particles.

This is why each of the four colligative properties is written in terms of the amount of solute only:

\(\Delta P = P_1^0x_2\), \(\Delta T_b = K_bm\), \(\Delta T_f = K_fm\), \(\pi = MRT\)

The nature of the solute appears in none of them. The nature of the solvent enters only through the constants \(K_b\) and \(K_f\), which are properties of the solvent itself and not of the solution, and the amount of solvent fixes the molality rather than being what the property counts.

For an electrolyte the count of particles rises, because one formula unit gives more than one ion in solution, and that is allowed for by the van't Hoff factor \(i\).

answer:
**(C)** ebullioscopy

The determination of the molar mass of a solute from the **elevation of the boiling point** of its solution is called ebullioscopy, after \(K_b\), the ebullioscopic constant. It rests on

\(\Delta T_b = K_bm = K_b\dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\) so that \(M_2 = \dfrac{1000\,K_b\mathrm{W_2}}{\Delta T_b\,\mathrm{W_1}}\)

The corresponding method built on the **depression of the freezing point** and the cryoscopic constant \(K_f\) is cryoscopy, so that name belongs to the other property. Colorimetry compares the intensity of colour of a solution and spectroscopy studies its absorption or emission of radiation; neither measures a colligative property, so neither can give a molar mass by this route.

answer:
**a. Molality.** The molality of a solution is the **number of moles of solute dissolved in one kilogram of solvent**.

\(m = \dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}} = \dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

where \(\mathrm{W_2}\) g of a solute of molar mass \(M_2\) is dissolved in \(\mathrm{W_1}\) g of solvent. Its unit is \(\mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\). Because molality is built on a **mass** of solvent, it does not change with temperature, and that is why it is the concentration unit used for boiling point elevation and freezing point depression.

**b. Osmotic pressure.** The osmotic pressure of a solution is the **pressure that has to be applied to the solution to stop osmosis**, that is, to stop the net flow of solvent into the solution through a semipermeable membrane separating it from the pure solvent.

For a dilute solution

\(\pi = MRT\)

where \(M\) is the molarity of the solution, \(R\) the gas constant and \(T\) the temperature in kelvin. Osmotic pressure is not a pressure that the solution exerts by itself; it appears only when the solution and the solvent are separated by a semipermeable membrane.

answer:
**(B)** molarity

Osmotic pressure is calculated from the van't Hoff equation for a dilute solution,

\(\pi V = n_2RT\) or \(\pi = MRT\)

in which \(M\) is the **molarity**, the number of moles of solute present in one \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) of **solution**. The volume of the solution is what enters the equation, and molarity is the concentration term built on that volume.

Molality is built on the mass of solvent and is used for boiling point elevation and freezing point depression, where the temperature changes during the measurement and a temperature-independent unit is needed. An osmotic pressure measurement is made at one fixed temperature, so the expansion of the solution does not matter and molarity may safely be used. Mole fraction and mass percentage do not appear in the equation for \(\pi\) at all.

answer:
**Isotonic solutions** are two or more solutions that have the **same osmotic pressure** at the same temperature.

Since \(\pi = iMRT\), two solutions are isotonic when the product \(iM\) is the same for both at that temperature. For nonelectrolytes \(i = 1\), so \(0.1\ \mathrm{M}\) urea and \(0.1\ \mathrm{M}\) sucrose are isotonic, even though their concentrations expressed in \(\mathrm{g\ dm^{-3}}\) are quite different.

When two isotonic solutions are separated by a semipermeable membrane there is **no net flow of solvent** in either direction, because the tendency of the solvent to pass one way is exactly balanced by its tendency to pass the other. A \(0.9\%\) solution of sodium chloride is isotonic with the fluid inside a red blood cell, which is why it is the solution used for a saline drip.

answer:
The cryoscopic constant, or freezing point depression constant \(K_f\), is defined by

\(\Delta T_f = K_fm\) so that \(K_f = \dfrac{\Delta T_f}{m}\)

Here \(\Delta T_f\) is a difference of temperature, measured in kelvin, and \(m\) is the molality, measured in \(\mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\). Dividing one unit by the other,

\(K_f = \dfrac{\mathrm{K}}{\mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}} = \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(\therefore\) the SI unit of the cryoscopic constant is \(\mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\).

Numerically \(K_f\) is the depression of freezing point produced by a one molal solution; for water its value is \(1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\).

answer:
Osmosis is the **spontaneous flow of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane** from the pure solvent into a solution, or from a dilute solution into a more concentrated one.

A semipermeable membrane, such as parchment, cellophane or the membrane of a living cell, has pores that let the small solvent molecules pass through but hold back the larger solute particles.

Solvent molecules in fact cross the membrane in **both** directions, but they leave the pure solvent faster than they leave the solution, because at the surface of the solution part of the area is occupied by solute particles and the mole fraction of solvent is smaller. The **net** flow is therefore into the solution. The level on the solution side rises until the hydrostatic pressure of the extra column stops the net flow, and that pressure is the osmotic pressure of the solution.

answer:
Henry's law states that **the solubility of a gas in a liquid at constant temperature is directly proportional to the pressure of the gas above the solution**.

If \(S\) is the solubility of the gas, expressed as its concentration in the solution, and \(P\) is the partial pressure of that gas over the solution, then

\(S \propto P\) or \(S = \mathrm{K_H}P\)

where \(\mathrm{K_H}\) is the Henry's law constant, of unit \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ bar^{-1}}\). Its value depends on the nature of the gas, the nature of the solvent and the temperature.

The law holds for a gas that does not react with the solvent, and at low pressures; a gas such as \(\mathrm{HCl}\) or \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), which reacts with water, does not obey it. It explains why a bottle of soda water fizzes when it is opened: the partial pressure of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) above the liquid falls, the solubility falls with it, and the excess gas escapes.

The osmotic pressure of a solution is the **hydrostatic pressure that builds up on the solution and stops osmosis**, that is, the pressure that stops the net flow of solvent into the solution through a semipermeable membrane separating it from the pure solvent. Equivalently, it is the external pressure which, applied to the solution, just prevents solvent from entering it.

For a dilute solution the van't Hoff equation gives

\(\pi V = n_2RT\) or \(\pi = MRT\)

where \(n_2\) is the number of moles of solute in volume \(V\) of solution, \(M\) is the molarity, \(R\) the gas constant and \(T\) the temperature in kelvin. For an electrolyte, which supplies more particles than formula units, \(\pi = iMRT\).

Osmotic pressure is a colligative property, since only the concentration of particles enters the equation and their nature does not, and it exists only while the solution is separated from the solvent by a semipermeable membrane.

answer:
\(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) is an electrolyte, so its osmotic pressure carries the van't Hoff factor:

\(\pi = iMRT = i\dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}RT}{M_2V}\)

\(\pi = 0.75\ \mathrm{atm},\ i = 2.47,\ V = 2.5\ \mathrm{dm^3},\ M_2 = 111\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}},\ R = 0.0821\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}},\ T = 300\ \mathrm{K}\)

Rearranging for the mass of solute,

\(\mathrm{W_2} = \dfrac{\pi VM_2}{iRT}\)

\(\mathrm{W_2} = \dfrac{0.75\ \mathrm{atm} \times 2.5\ \mathrm{dm^3} \times 111\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}}{2.47 \times 0.0821\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 300\ \mathrm{K}}\)

\(= \dfrac{208.125}{60.84}\ \mathrm{g}\)

\(\therefore \mathrm{W_2} = 3.42\ \mathrm{g}\)

Check: \(3.42\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) is \(3.42/111 = 0.0308\ \mathrm{mol}\), so the molarity is \(0.0308/2.5 = 0.01233\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), and \(\pi = 2.47 \times 0.01233 \times 0.0821 \times 300 = 0.75\ \mathrm{atm}\), the pressure given.

The value \(1.6 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\) printed in the stem cannot be that constant, because with it the first experiment would give a depression of \(2.7 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{K}\) and not the \(0.21\ \mathrm{K}\) stated beside it. | | urea | second solute |

\(\dfrac{60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.21\ \mathrm{K} \times 998\ \mathrm{g}}{10\ \mathrm{g}} = \dfrac{M_2' \times 0.34\ \mathrm{K} \times 86\ \mathrm{g}}{1.6\ \mathrm{g}}\)

answer:
For a dilute solution of a nonvolatile solute, Raoult's law gives the relative lowering of vapour pressure as

\(\dfrac{P_1^0 - P_1}{P_1^0} = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2} \times M_1}{M_2 \times \mathrm{W_1}}\)

\(P_1^0 = 640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg},\ P_1 = 600\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg},\ \mathrm{W_2} = 2.175 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg} = 2.175\ \mathrm{g},\ \mathrm{W_1} = 39\ \mathrm{g}\)

Benzene is \(\mathrm{C_6H_6}\), so with \(\mathrm{C} = 12\) and \(\mathrm{H} = 1\),

\(M_1 = 6 \times 12 + 6 \times 1 = 78\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Substituting,

\(\dfrac{640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} - 600\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}}{640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}} = \dfrac{2.175\ \mathrm{g} \times 78\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}}{M_2 \times 39\ \mathrm{g}}\)

\(\dfrac{40}{640} = 0.0625 = \dfrac{2.175 \times 78}{M_2 \times 39}\)

Rearranging for the molar mass,

\(M_2 = \dfrac{2.175\ \mathrm{g} \times 78\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}} \times 640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}}{40\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} \times 39\ \mathrm{g}}\)

\(\therefore M_2 = 69.6\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Check: \(2.175\ \mathrm{g}\) of a solute of molar mass \(69.6\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) is \(0.03125\ \mathrm{mol}\), and \(39\ \mathrm{g}\) of benzene is \(0.5\ \mathrm{mol}\). The exact mole fraction of solute is then \(0.03125/0.53125 = 0.0588\), and Raoult's law gives \(P_1 = 640(1 - 0.0588) = 602\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\), close to the \(600\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\) measured; the small difference is the dilute-solution approximation used in the working formula.

answer:
For a dilute solution the van't Hoff equation is

\(\pi V = n_2RT = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2}RT\) so \(M_2 = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}RT}{\pi V}\)

\(R\) is given here in \(\mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), so \(\pi\) and \(V\) are taken in SI units to match it:

\(\pi = 0.52\ \mathrm{atm} = 0.52 \times 101325\ \mathrm{Pa} = 5.269 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{Pa}\)

\(V = 1\ \mathrm{dm^3} = 1 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}\)

\(\mathrm{W_2} = 1.8 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg} = 1.8\ \mathrm{g},\ T = 286\ \mathrm{K}\)

Substituting,

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1.8\ \mathrm{g} \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 286\ \mathrm{K}}{5.269 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{Pa} \times 1 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}} = \dfrac{4280\ \mathrm{g\ J\ mol^{-1}}}{52.69\ \mathrm{J}}\)

\(\therefore M_2 = 81.2\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Check by the other set of units: with \(R = 0.08206\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), \(\pi = 0.52\ \mathrm{atm}\) and \(V = 1\ \mathrm{dm^3}\),

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1.8 \times 0.08206 \times 286}{0.52 \times 1} = 81.2\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

the same value, so the conversion of atmospheres to pascals and of \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) to \(\mathrm{m^3}\) has been made consistently.

answer:
The elevation of boiling point is

\(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^0 = 354.11\ \mathrm{K} - 353.23\ \mathrm{K} = 0.88\ \mathrm{K}\)

For a dilute solution of a nonvolatile solute,

\(\Delta T_b = K_bm = K_b\dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\) so \(M_2 = \dfrac{1000\,K_b\mathrm{W_2}}{\Delta T_b\,\mathrm{W_1}}\)

\(K_b = 2.53\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}},\ \mathrm{W_2} = 1.80\ \mathrm{g},\ \mathrm{W_1} = 90\ \mathrm{g},\ \Delta T_b = 0.88\ \mathrm{K}\)

Substituting,

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1000\ \mathrm{g\ kg^{-1}} \times 2.53\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}} \times 1.80\ \mathrm{g}}{0.88\ \mathrm{K} \times 90\ \mathrm{g}} = \dfrac{4554}{79.2}\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(\therefore M_2 = 57.5\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Check: \(1.80\ \mathrm{g}\) of a solute of molar mass \(57.5\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) is \(0.0313\ \mathrm{mol}\), dissolved in \(0.090\ \mathrm{kg}\) of benzene, a molality of \(0.348\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\). Then \(\Delta T_b = 2.53 \times 0.348 = 0.88\ \mathrm{K}\), which is the rise from \(353.23\ \mathrm{K}\) to \(354.11\ \mathrm{K}\) given.

answer:
**(A)** \(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}\)

For an electrolyte solution the osmotic pressure is

\(\pi = iMRT\)

All four solutions are \(0.1\ \mathrm{M}\) and are at the same temperature, so \(M\), \(R\) and \(T\) are common to all four and \(\pi\) is decided by the van't Hoff factor \(i\) alone - that is, by the number of ions one formula unit gives on complete dissociation.

\(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{Al^{3+}} + 3\,\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\), \(i = 5\)

\(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{Na^{+}} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\), \(i = 3\)

\(\mathrm{MgCl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg^{2+}} + 2\,\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\), \(i = 3\)

\(\mathrm{KCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{K^{+}} + \mathrm{Cl^{-}}\), \(i = 2\)

Aluminium sulphate gives **five** particles per formula unit, the largest of the four, so its \(0.1\ \mathrm{M}\) solution exerts the highest osmotic pressure.

At \(298\ \mathrm{K}\) the four pressures work out as \(12.2\), \(7.34\), \(7.34\) and \(4.89\ \mathrm{atm}\), standing in the ratio \(5 : 3 : 3 : 2\) of their van't Hoff factors.

answer:
By Henry's law, the solubility of a gas in a liquid at constant temperature is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas above the solution:

\(S = \mathrm{K_H}P\)

\(\mathrm{K_H} = 0.159\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ bar^{-1}},\ P = 0.164\ \mathrm{bar}\)

The temperature of the measurement, \(25\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), is the temperature at which \(\mathrm{K_H}\) is quoted, so the constant may be used as it stands.

\(S = 0.159\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ bar^{-1}} \times 0.164\ \mathrm{bar}\)

\(\therefore S = 0.0261\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\)

Check: the units multiply out to \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), which is a concentration as it must be. The partial pressure is a little under one sixth of a bar, so the solubility should come out a little under one sixth of \(0.159\), and \(0.0261\) is.

answer:
For a solution of a nonvolatile solute, Raoult's law gives \(P_1 = P_1^0x_1\), and in a binary solution \(x_1 + x_2 = 1\), so

\(P_1 = P_1^0(1 - x_2) = P_1^0 - P_1^0x_2\)

\(P_1^0 - P_1 = P_1^0x_2\) so \(\dfrac{P_1^0 - P_1}{P_1^0} = x_2\)

The relative lowering of vapour pressure is therefore equal to the mole fraction of the solute.

\(P_1^0 = 640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg},\ P_1 = 600\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

\(x_2 = \dfrac{640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} - 600\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}}{640\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}} = \dfrac{40}{640}\)

\(\therefore x_2 = 0.0625\)

Check: the mole fraction of the solvent is then \(x_1 = 1 - 0.0625 = 0.9375\), and Raoult's law returns \(P_1 = 640 \times 0.9375 = 600\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\), the vapour pressure of the solution given.

answer:
Henry's law relates the solubility of a gas to its partial pressure above the solution at constant temperature:

\(S = \mathrm{K_H}P\)

where \(S\) is the solubility expressed as a concentration and \(\mathrm{K_H}\) is the Henry's law constant of the gas in that solvent at that temperature.

\(\mathrm{K_H} = 0.159\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ bar^{-1}}\)

\(P = 0.164\ \mathrm{bar}\)

Both the constant and the required solubility refer to \(25\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), so no correction for temperature is needed.

\(S = 0.159\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ bar^{-1}} \times 0.164\ \mathrm{bar}\)

\(\therefore S = 0.0261\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), that is \(0.0261\ \mathrm{M}\)

Check: rearranging, \(\mathrm{K_H} = S/P = 0.0261/0.164 = 0.159\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ bar^{-1}}\), which returns the constant given.

answer:
Urea, \(\mathrm{NH_2CONH_2}\), is a nonelectrolyte, so it does not dissociate in water and \(i = 1\). The depression of freezing point is therefore

\(\Delta T_f = K_fm\)

\(K_f = 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}},\ m = 0.1\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

\(\Delta T_f = 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.1\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}} = 0.186\ \mathrm{K}\)

Pure water freezes at \(T_f^0 = 273.15\ \mathrm{K}\), that is \(0\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), and the solution freezes lower by \(\Delta T_f\):

\(T_f = T_f^0 - \Delta T_f = 273.15\ \mathrm{K} - 0.186\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(\therefore T_f = 272.96\ \mathrm{K}\), that is \(-0.186\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)

Check: the solution is one tenth molal, so its depression must be one tenth of \(K_f\) itself, and \(0.186\) is one tenth of \(1.86\).

\(\mathrm{KBr}\) is a strong electrolyte, and is taken here to be **completely dissociated** in water:

\(\mathrm{KBr} \longrightarrow \mathrm{K^{+}} + \mathrm{Br^{-}}\)

One mole of \(\mathrm{KBr}\) therefore gives two moles of ions, so

\(i = \dfrac{\text{moles of particles after dissociation}}{\text{moles of formula units dissolved}} = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2\)

Pure water freezes at \(0\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), so the depression of freezing point is

\(\Delta T_f = T_f^0 - T_f = 0\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C} - (-3.72\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}) = 3.72\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C} = 3.72\ \mathrm{K}\)

For an electrolyte, \(\Delta T_f = iK_fm\), so

\(m = \dfrac{\Delta T_f}{iK_f} = \dfrac{3.72\ \mathrm{K}}{2 \times 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}}\)

\(\therefore m = 1.00\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

Check: a one molal \(\mathrm{KBr}\) solution supplies two moles of ions per kilogram of water, so \(\Delta T_f = 1.86 \times 2 \times 1.00 = 3.72\ \mathrm{K}\), which puts the freezing point at \(-3.72\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) as given.

The depression of freezing point of a dilute solution of a nonvolatile nonelectrolyte is directly proportional to the molality of the solution:

\(\Delta T_f = K_fm\)

If \(\mathrm{W_2}\) g of the solute, of molar mass \(M_2\), is dissolved in \(\mathrm{W_1}\) g of solvent, then

moles of solute \(= \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2}\), mass of solvent \(= \dfrac{\mathrm{W_1}}{1000}\ \mathrm{kg}\)

answer:
Raoult's law for a solution containing a nonvolatile solute gives the vapour pressure of the solution as

\(P_1 = P_1^0x_1\)

where \(x_1\) is the mole fraction of the solvent and \(P_1^0\) the vapour pressure of the pure solvent.

The solution is binary, so \(x_1 + x_2 = 1\), that is \(x_1 = 1 - x_2\). Substituting,

\(P_1 = P_1^0(1 - x_2) = P_1^0 - P_1^0x_2\)

\(P_1^0 - P_1 = P_1^0x_2\)

Dividing throughout by \(P_1^0\),

\(\dfrac{P_1^0 - P_1}{P_1^0} = x_2\)

The left-hand side is the **relative lowering of vapour pressure**, so it is equal to the mole fraction of the solute.

Now let \(\mathrm{W_2}\) g of the solute of molar mass \(M_2\) be dissolved in \(\mathrm{W_1}\) g of a solvent of molar mass \(M_1\). Then

\(n_2 = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2}\), \(n_1 = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_1}}{M_1}\), \(x_2 = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1 + n_2}\)

For a dilute solution \(n_2\) is very small beside \(n_1\), so \(n_1 + n_2 \approx n_1\), and

\(x_2 = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}/M_2}{\mathrm{W_1}/M_1} = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}M_1}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\)

Hence

\(\dfrac{P_1^0 - P_1}{P_1^0} = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}M_1}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\)

\(\therefore M_2 = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}M_1P_1^0}{(P_1^0 - P_1)\,\mathrm{W_1}}\)

This is the required relation. Measuring \(P_1^0\) and \(P_1\) for a solution made from known masses \(\mathrm{W_2}\) and \(\mathrm{W_1}\), with \(M_1\) of the solvent known, gives the molar mass of the solute.
twin: Using Raoult's law, how will you show that \(\Delta P = P_1^0 x_2\) ? Where \(x_2\) is the mole fraction of solute in the solution and \(P_1^0\) vapour pressure of pure solvent.

The elevation of boiling point of a dilute solution is directly proportional to its molality:

\(\Delta T_b \propto m\) so \(\Delta T_b = K_bm\)

where \(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^0\) is the difference between the boiling point of the solution and that of the pure solvent, and \(K_b\) is the boiling point elevation constant, or ebullioscopic constant, of the solvent, of unit \(\mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\).

Let \(\mathrm{W_2}\) g of a nonvolatile solute of molar mass \(M_2\) be dissolved in \(\mathrm{W_1}\) g of the solvent. Then

moles of solute \(= \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2}\), mass of solvent \(= \dfrac{\mathrm{W_1}}{1000}\ \mathrm{kg}\)

so the molality of the solution is

\(m = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}/M_2}{\mathrm{W_1}/1000} = \dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

Substituting this in \(\Delta T_b = K_bm\),

\(\Delta T_b = K_b\dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\)

and rearranging for the molar mass,

\(\therefore M_2 = \dfrac{1000\,K_b\mathrm{W_2}}{\Delta T_b\,\mathrm{W_1}}\)

This is the required relation between the elevation of boiling point and the molar mass of the solute.

answer:
The van't Hoff general solution equation is obtained by combining the three laws that the osmotic pressure of a dilute solution obeys.

**1. van't Hoff-Boyle law.** At constant temperature, the osmotic pressure of a dilute solution is directly proportional to its concentration, that is, inversely proportional to the volume of solution in which a fixed amount of solute is dissolved:

\(\pi \propto \dfrac{1}{V}\) at constant \(n\) and \(T\)

**2. van't Hoff-Charles law.** At constant concentration, the osmotic pressure is directly proportional to the absolute temperature:

\(\pi \propto T\) at constant \(n\) and \(V\)

**3. Dependence on the amount of solute.** At constant volume and temperature, the osmotic pressure is directly proportional to the number of moles of solute dissolved:

\(\pi \propto n\) at constant \(V\) and \(T\)

Combining the three proportionalities,

\(\pi \propto \dfrac{nT}{V}\)

Introducing a constant of proportionality \(R\),

\(\pi = \dfrac{nRT}{V}\)

\(\therefore \pi V = nRT\)

This is the van't Hoff general solution equation. It has exactly the form of the ideal gas equation, and \(R\) is found by experiment to have the same value, \(0.08206\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), which is why a solute in a dilute solution is said to behave as a gas would if it occupied the volume of the solution.

Since \(n/V\) is the molarity \(M\), the equation is also written \(\pi = MRT\), and for an electrolyte giving \(i\) particles per formula unit, \(\pi = iMRT\).

answer:
**Molar mass from the elevation of boiling point.**

The elevation of boiling point of a dilute solution of a nonvolatile solute is directly proportional to the molality of the solution:

\(\Delta T_b = K_bm\)

where \(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^0\) and \(K_b\) is the ebullioscopic constant of the solvent.

If \(\mathrm{W_2}\) g of the solute, of molar mass \(M_2\), is dissolved in \(\mathrm{W_1}\) g of solvent, the molality is

\(m = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}/M_2}{\mathrm{W_1}/1000} = \dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

Substituting,

\(\Delta T_b = K_b\dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\)

\(\therefore M_2 = \dfrac{1000\,K_b\mathrm{W_2}}{\Delta T_b\,\mathrm{W_1}}\)

which is the required expression connecting the molar mass of the solute with the elevation of boiling point.

**van't Hoff-Avogadro law.**

*Statement:* Equal volumes of dilute solutions of different solutes, having the same osmotic pressure at the same temperature, contain the **same number of solute particles**, that is, the same number of moles of solute.

*Explanation:* By the van't Hoff general solution equation,

\(\pi V = n_2RT\) so \(n_2 = \dfrac{\pi V}{RT}\)

Take two solutions of different solutes with the same osmotic pressure \(\pi\), the same volume \(V\) and the same temperature \(T\). Then

\(n_2 = \dfrac{\pi V}{RT}\) and \(n_2' = \dfrac{\pi V}{RT}\) so \(n_2 = n_2'\)

The two solutions therefore contain equal numbers of moles of solute, whatever those solutes are. This is the exact counterpart, for solutions, of Avogadro's law for gases, in which equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. It is the basis of isotonic solutions: two solutions of equal osmotic pressure at the same temperature have equal molar concentrations of particles.

answer:
For a dilute solution the osmotic pressure obeys the van't Hoff general solution equation

\(\pi V = n_2RT\)

where \(n_2\) is the number of moles of solute present in volume \(V\) of solution, \(R\) is the gas constant and \(T\) the temperature in kelvin.

If \(\mathrm{W_2}\) g of the solute has molar mass \(M_2\), then

\(n_2 = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2}\)

Substituting this in the equation above,

\(\pi V = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}RT}{M_2}\) so \(\pi = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}RT}{M_2V}\)

\(\therefore M_2 = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}RT}{\pi V}\)

This is the required expression. A known mass \(\mathrm{W_2}\) of the nonvolatile solute is dissolved to make a known volume \(V\) of solution, the osmotic pressure \(\pi\) of that solution is measured at a known temperature \(T\), and the molar mass follows on substitution. The units must match: with \(\pi\) in atmospheres and \(V\) in \(\mathrm{dm^3}\), \(R = 0.08206\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\).

For an electrolyte the equation carries the van't Hoff factor, \(M_2 = i\,\mathrm{W_2}RT/(\pi V)\).

The method is the one preferred for substances of large molar mass, such as proteins and polymers, because even a very dilute solution of them develops an osmotic pressure large enough to be measured accurately, while its elevation of boiling point would be far too small to detect.

answer:
**Principle.** The elevation of boiling point of a dilute solution is directly proportional to its molality,

\(\Delta T_b = K_bm = K_b\dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\)

\(\therefore M_2 = \dfrac{1000\,K_b\mathrm{W_2}}{\Delta T_b\,\mathrm{W_1}}\)

where \(\mathrm{W_2}\) g of solute of molar mass \(M_2\) is dissolved in \(\mathrm{W_1}\) g of a solvent whose ebullioscopic constant is \(K_b\).

**Procedure.**

1. A known mass \(\mathrm{W_2}\) of the nonvolatile solute is dissolved in a known mass \(\mathrm{W_1}\) of a solvent for which \(K_b\) is known.
2. The boiling point \(T_b^0\) of the pure solvent and the boiling point \(T_b\) of the solution are measured at the same applied pressure, with a thermometer that can read small differences of temperature.
3. The elevation is obtained as \(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^0\).
4. \(K_b\), \(\mathrm{W_2}\), \(\mathrm{W_1}\) and \(\Delta T_b\) are substituted in the expression above to give \(M_2\).

**Example.** \(1.80\ \mathrm{g}\) of a solute in \(90\ \mathrm{g}\) of benzene, for which \(K_b = 2.53\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\), raises the boiling point by \(0.88\ \mathrm{K}\). Then

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1000 \times 2.53 \times 1.80}{0.88 \times 90} = 57.5\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

The method assumes the solution is dilute, that the solute is nonvolatile, and that it neither dissociates nor associates in the solvent. If it does, the value obtained is the observed molar mass, and the true molar mass follows from it through the van't Hoff factor.

\(\pi V = n_2RT = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2}RT\)

\(\therefore M_2 = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}RT}{\pi V}\)

where \(\mathrm{W_2}\) g of solute of molar mass \(M_2\) is dissolved to make volume \(V\) of solution, \(\pi\) is the osmotic pressure at temperature \(T\), and \(R\) is the gas constant.

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1.8 \times 0.08206 \times 286}{0.52 \times 1} = 81.2\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

answer:
**Raoult's law** for a solution containing a nonvolatile solute states that the vapour pressure of the solvent over the solution is equal to the vapour pressure of the pure solvent multiplied by the mole fraction of the solvent in the solution.

Consider a binary solution made of a solvent and one nonvolatile solute. Let

\(P_1^0\) = vapour pressure of the pure solvent, \(P_1\) = vapour pressure of the solvent over the solution,

\(x_1\) = mole fraction of the solvent, \(x_2\) = mole fraction of the solute.

Because the solute is nonvolatile it contributes nothing to the vapour above the solution, so \(P_1\) is also the vapour pressure of the **solution**. Raoult's law is then

\(P_1 = P_1^0x_1\)

The solution is binary, so the two mole fractions add to unity:

\(x_1 + x_2 = 1\) so \(x_1 = 1 - x_2\)

Substituting this in the law,

\(P_1 = P_1^0(1 - x_2) = P_1^0 - P_1^0x_2\)

Rearranging,

\(P_1^0 - P_1 = P_1^0x_2\)

The left-hand side is the lowering of vapour pressure, \(\Delta P = P_1^0 - P_1\), so

\(\therefore \Delta P = P_1^0x_2\) and \(\dfrac{P_1^0 - P_1}{P_1^0} = x_2\)

These are the working equations of Raoult's law for such a solution. Since \(P_1^0\) is a constant at a given temperature, the lowering of vapour pressure depends only on \(x_2\), the mole fraction of the solute, and not on what the solute is - which is why the lowering of vapour pressure is a colligative property.
